name: ePrivacy Directive
evidence_rating: moderate: one influential peer-reviewed causal study; Commission evaluation with acknowledged data gaps
summary: The ePrivacy Directive set no measurable targets. The Commission's own 2017 evaluation found its cookie-consent rule had not given users real control and was over-inclusive, at around EUR 658 compliance cost per business. Independent research found the EU tracking rules made online display advertising markedly less effective, especially for news sites. The proposed ePrivacy Regulation meant to fix this was withdrawn in 2025.

indicators.objective: 2000 proposal (COM(2000) 385) predates standard indicators sections; no quantified objectives or indicators were set
Confidentiality of communications / user control (cookie rule)
indicators.evidence: Commission REFIT evaluation (2017): cookie rule 'not fully effective' - users accept tracking without understanding it, some cookies set without consent; rule also over-inclusive for non-privacy-intrusive cookies.
Supporting study estimates about EUR 658 per business; Commission notes robust cost data largely do not exist.

literature.citation: European Commission (2017), Ex-post REFIT evaluation of the ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC (executive summary SWD(2017) 6), SWD(2017) 5
literature.title: Ex-post REFIT evaluation of the ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC (executive summary SWD(2017) 6)
literature.headline: Directive broadly appropriate but enforcement fragmented; cookie rule not fully effective and over-inclusive; compliance costs around EUR 658 per business; robust cost data lacking
literature.summary_plain: The Commission found the cookie consent rule had not really given people control - they click 'accept' without understanding - while costing businesses a few hundred euros each.

literature.citation: Goldfarb & Tucker (2011), Privacy Regulation and Online Advertising, Management Science 57(1)
literature.title: Privacy Regulation and Online Advertising
literature.method: causal: difference-in-differences (3.3m survey takers, 9,596 ad campaigns; EU vs other countries)
literature.headline: After the EU privacy rules (ePrivacy Directive) took effect, display advertising became far less effective at changing purchase intent relative to other countries; larger losses for general-content sites such as news and for plain, small ads
literature.summary_plain: Early EU privacy rules on tracking made online display ads much less effective, hitting news sites hardest.
literature.quality: measures ad effectiveness (stated purchase intent), not revenue

literature.citation: Alexander Egberts, Julia Krämer (2026), Privacy concerns and choices under design friction: Evidence from cookie consent banners, Information Economics and Policy
literature.title: Privacy concerns and choices under design friction: Evidence from cookie consent banners
literature.method: preregistered online experiment with 1,142 German internet users varying how refusal is presented in cookie banners
literature.headline: Banner designs that make refusal harder weaken the link between users' stated privacy concerns and their consent choices, undermining consent as a signal of preferences.

literature.citation: Luca Congiu, Ivan Moscati, Matteo Scacchi (2022), Digital Nudging and Cookie Rejection: An Experiment, Italian Economic Journal
literature.authors: Luca Congiu, Ivan Moscati, Matteo Scacchi
literature.title: Digital Nudging and Cookie Rejection: An Experiment
literature.method: online experiment (n = 358) testing salience and framing nudges in a cookie banner
literature.headline: Against a 27% baseline rejection rate, framing raised rejection by 18 points and salience plus framing by 53 points; only 3% used a customise option to reject.

literature.citation: Martino Trevisan, Stefano Traverso, Eleonora Bassi, Marco Mellia (2019), 4 Years of EU Cookie Law: Results and Lessons Learned, Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies 2019(2)
literature.authors: Martino Trevisan, Stefano Traverso, Eleonora Bassi, Marco Mellia
literature.title: 4 Years of EU Cookie Law: Results and Lessons Learned
literature.method: large-scale crawl of about 35,000 websites checking whether profiling cookies are set before consent
literature.headline: Four years after the cookie rule became mandatory, about half of websites still set profiling cookies before obtaining consent.

literature.citation: Armitage, C., Botton, N., Dejeu-Castang, L. & Lemoine, L., for the European Commission (DG CNECT) (2023), Study on the impact of recent developments in digital advertising on privacy, publishers and advertisers, Publications Office of the European Union
literature.authors: Armitage, C., Botton, N., Dejeu-Castang, L. & Lemoine, L., for the European Commission (DG CNECT)
literature.title: Study on the impact of recent developments in digital advertising on privacy, publishers and advertisers
literature.venue: Publications Office of the European Union
literature.method: desk research, market data, interviews and stakeholder consultation (274-page report)
literature.headline: The evidence on balance indicates a strong case to reform digital advertising: lack of transparency, publishers' weak position against data-rich platforms, and harms from tracking-based profiling.
